title: Semantically Orthogonal Framework for Citation Classification: Disentangling Intent and Content

With fine-tuning, however, Cited Content Type becomes more learnable (Qwen-Small F 1 F_{1} : 0.78 vs. 0.65 for intent), indicating its distinctions benefit more from supervision. Cross-domain generalization is competitive for both dimensions, with fine-tuned Qwen showing only modest performance drops on both content (Qwen-Small: 18%; SciBERT: 41%) and intent (Qwen-Small: 14%; SciBERT: 62%). This highlights SOFT’s stability under domain shift and the superior transferability of fine-tuned Qwen over SciBERT. Across all experiments, the SOFT framework consistently outperforms ACL-ARC and SciCite in interpretability, learnability, and cross-domain robustness. Fine-tuned Qwen-Small achieves the best results on Cited Content Type , while Qwen zero-shot achieves top performance on Citation Intent . These findings establish SOFT as a semantically orthogonal and generalizable alternative for citation annotation. This paper introduces the SOFT framework, a semantically orthogonal framework with two dimensions for citation annotation that disentangles cited content type from citation intent . By addressing the conceptual conflation and boundary ambiguity in existing frameworks, SOFT provides clearer interpretive definitions and better supports both human annotation and model-based classification. Empirical evaluations across LLM agreement, in-domain classification, and cross-domain generalization confirm SOFT’s advantages. The citation intent dimension demonstrates high zero-shot and fine-tuned performance, while the cited content type dimension, despite its semantic complexity, proves learnable and transferable.
